changes.after: A pointer stays useful only while its target exists. A local static variable lasts for the whole program.

before: A block-local ordinary object has automatic storage duration: its lifetime ends when execution leaves its block. Returning its address would not extend that lifetime. Do not read through a dangling pointer.

A block-local static object exists for the entire program and is initialized once. Returning its address is valid, but callers share that same object. ++n adds one and stores it; this single-threaded example keeps the count small.

Expected output or behavior: 2
. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Call counter a third time and explain why all returned pointers refer to one object. You may trace it without a C compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: An ordinary local variable exists only until its block ends. Returning its address does not keep it alive. A pointer left referring to an object whose life has ended is called dangling. Do not use it to read or write.
A local variable marked static lasts for the whole program. Its starting value is set once. Every call here uses the same n. `++n` adds 1 before the function returns its address.
The first call changes n from 0 to 1. The second changes the same n to 2. first still points to that shared variable, so the print displays 2. This example has only one thread of work.
Remove the second call. The shared n is then increased only once. first still points to a live static variable.

before.question: If the second counter() call is removed, what does *first print?
before.explanation: Both calls access the same static n. With only the first call, it has been incremented once from zero.

after.question: Remove the second counter() call. What does *first print?
choices: A value from a dangling pointer.
after.explanation: n starts at 0 and increases once to 1. It is static, so it stays alive after counter returns.
